playground.label: Where does the pointer end? The screen arithmetic of PyAutoGUI on a 1920 by 1080 screen, written in plain Python: positions start at 0, the pointer stops at the edge, and the four corners are the fail-safe points (no mouse is moved)
playground.code:
width, height = 1920, 1080
raw = input('Where should the pointer go? x, y (try 5000, 5000 and then -50, -50): ')
x, y = (int(n) for n in raw.split(','))

def clamp(value, low, high):
    return max(low, min(high, value))

def on_screen(px, py):
    return 0 <= px < width and 0 <= py < height

print('screen size:', (width, height))
print('corners:', [(0, 0), (width - 1, 0), (0, height - 1), (width - 1, height - 1)])
print('fail-safe points are the same four corners')
print('on screen:', on_screen(x, y))
print('the pointer would stop at:', (clamp(x, 0, width - 1), clamp(y, 0, height - 1)))
print('a call after reaching a corner raises FailSafeException:', (clamp(x, 0, width - 1), clamp(y, 0, height - 1)) in [(0, 0), (width - 1, 0), (0, height - 1), (width - 1, height - 1)])

findings: A missing image

With PyScreeze 0.1.27, 0.1.28 and 0.1.29 a missing image returns None and click('submit.png') raises TypeError: cannot unpack non-iterable NoneType object, while with 0.1.30, 1.0.0 and 1.0.1 it raises ImageNotFoundException, so the change is at PyScreeze 0.1.30; PyAutoGUI 0.9.41 with PyScreeze 1.0.1 and 0.9.40 do not import, and hold() exists from 0.9.54 and not in 0.9.41 or 0.9.50 (MEASURED single runs) [P11] [P16] [P17].
Appendix B

The answer to question 6 types Hello world! without the comma of the question, the answer to question 13 misspells pyautogui as pyatuogui (NameError) and calls activate on a list, and the answer to question 1 says to move the mouse to any corner, which raises FailSafeException in the next call; the answers to 13 questions were read on the page, 252,727 bytes [P06].
Backends and permissions

The 3 backends name SendInput, mouse_event and keybd_event (Windows), CGEventPost and Quartz (macOS) and fake_input of XTEST (Linux); with XDG_SESSION_TYPE set to wayland a screenshot raised PyScreezeException while moveTo(300, 200) still worked through X; Windows documents SendInput as subject to UIPI and macOS asks for the accessibility permission, and none of the 3 input paths other than X11 ran here (NOT EXECUTED) [P33] [P35] [P36] [P38].
Background

Chapter 23 of the 3rd edition, Controlling the Keyboard and Mouse, teaches PyAutoGUI (the fail-safes, moving, clicking, dragging and scrolling the mouse, the MouseInfo application, screenshots, pixel colors, image recognition, window objects, typing and key names, hotkeys, tips for GUI scripts and message boxes) and ends with 13 practice questions and 3 practice programs [P01]. The page was fetched on 2026-10-13 and returned 200 with 103,072 bytes, holds 25 listings, 6 figures and 1 table, and its sha256 equals the chapterDigest the book's own chapter ontology records [P01] [P03] [P04].
Coordinates, steps and monitors

Points outside the screen are clamped by the X server, (-50, -50) giving (0, 0) and (5000, 5000) giving (1919, 1079), while (40000, 500) raises struct.error; a move of duration 0.25 made 6 motion events and 1.0 made 21; with 2 virtual monitors added xrandr listed 3 monitors and size() still said (1920, 1080), which fits the documentation that only the primary monitor is handled (MEASURED single runs) [P01] [P07] [P09].
Exact image matching

A button cut from the screen was found at (400, 300, 84, 35); the same image with one black pixel raised ImageNotFoundException, as the chapter says, and so did grayscale=True, confidence=0.9 found it only with OpenCV installed and raised NotImplementedError otherwise, the same button at a larger font, 109 by 45 pixels instead of 84 by 35, was not found, and a Box holds np.int64 with OpenCV and int without it (MEASURED single runs) [P01] [P11] [P50].
Interpreters and releases

One program of 27 items ran under 12 interpreter rows: Python 3.12.3, 3.13.14, 3.14.2 to 3.14.6, 3.15.0b4 and 3.14.6 with OpenCV ran every item, 3.14.0 and 3.14.1 raised TclError: Can't find a usable init.tcl, and 3.11.17 had no tkinter; 14 of the 27 items differed between some pair of rows; across 14 PyAutoGUI and PyScreeze combinations 7 items differed, across 7 Pillow releases (9.5.0 to 12.3.0) 3 items differed only by a DeprecationWarning in 12.3.0, and across 3 PyMsgBox releases the signatures differed [P20] [P30] [P54] [P55].
Looking busy and the idle time

The X idle time was reset by move(1, 0) and press('shift') (under 0.4 seconds) and not by position(), size() or screenshot() (over 1 second); a script that moved the pointer 1 pixel left and right three times made the x positions 799, 800, 799, 800, 799 and 800 and the idle time fell from above 2 seconds to below 1.5 seconds (MEASURED single runs) [P01] [P48].
Message boxes

Enter on alert and on confirm returned 'OK', Escape on confirm returned 'Cancel', prompt returned '' for Enter alone and None for Escape, password returned 's3cret', and confirm with timeout=1500 returned 'Timeout' after about 1.5 seconds; the installed PyMsgBox 2.0.1 says __version__ 1.0.9, and its signatures carry type hints that 1.0.9 lacks (MEASURED single runs) [P12] [P19] [P20].
MouseInfo and Tk 9

pyautogui.mouseInfo() ended with TclError: bad option 'variable' under Tk 9.0.3 (Python 3.13.14 to 3.15.0b4) and ran under Tk 8.6.14, where F6 with the 3 Sec. Button Delay on logged 1600,850 after the pointer had moved from 1500,800, and with the delay off logged 1500,800, 1600,850 and 1700,900; the Tcl 9.0 manual documents trace add variable and not the old trace variable (MEASURED single runs) [P01] [P24] [P40].
No release 1.0.0

The chapter attaches behaviour to PyAutoGUI 1.0.0 in 3 passages (locateOnScreen returning None before it, window features working only on Windows as of it, and the same note in the practice program), but PyPI lists 50 releases of PyAutoGUI with 0.9.54 (2023-05-24) as the newest and no 1.0.0, while PyScreeze, which does the locating, has 1.0.0 and 1.0.1 (both 2024-08-20) among its 29 releases; the installed set was PyAutoGUI 0.9.54, PyScreeze 1.0.1, PyMsgBox 2.0.1, PyTweening 1.2.0, PyGetWindow 0.0.9, MouseInfo 0.1.3 and python3-xlib 0.15 [P01] [P16] [P17].
Not executed

Nothing ran on Windows or macOS, with the accessibility permission, with a real Wayland compositor, on real or multiple monitors, with HiDPI scaling, on a real screen, in the Sushi Go Round game, against a captcha, or with a real instant messenger; Python 3.15 was only the beta 3.15.0b4; and the photograph was not fetched because the single request to Wikimedia Commons answered 429 [P01] [P36] [P43] [P55].
Pauses and fail-safes

PAUSE is 0.1 and 15 action functions pause after the call, 14 of them once and rightClick twice, while position, size, screenshot, pixel, onScreen and sleep do not; the corners (0, 0), (1919, 0), (0, 1079) and (1919, 1079) make the next call raise FailSafeException but moveTo(0, 0) itself returns, and afterwards position, size and screenshot still run while click, write and moveTo raise; FAILSAFE_POINTS is computed at import, so after the screen was resized from 1920 by 1080 to 1280 by 720 the running process kept the old corners (MEASURED single runs with PyAutoGUI 0.9.54) [P01] [P07] [P08].
Scroll units

scroll(-1), scroll(-2), scroll(-3) and scroll(-10) moved a text widget by 1, 3, 5 and 19 lines under Tk 9.0.3 and by 2, 5, 8 and 29 lines under Tk 8.6.14, while scroll(3) sent 3 presses of button 4, scroll(-2) 2 of button 5, hscroll(2) 2 of button 7 and hscroll(-1) 1 of button 6, so the chapter's advice to experiment holds (MEASURED single runs) [P01] [P09] [P27].
Silent key names

press('nokey'), press('SHIFT'), keyDown('nokey') and hotkey('ctrl', 'nokey') raised nothing and typed nothing, write(['a', 'nokey', 'b']) typed ab, write('café') typed caf, an emoji vanished and write(12) raised TypeError; KEYBOARD_KEYS holds 194 names, every one of the 41 names of Table 23-1 and its text is in it, f13 and f24 exist and the capital A is not in the list, and the roadmap lists a strict mode as a plan (MEASURED single runs) [P01] [P10] [P14].
The chapter replayed

The 25 listings of the chapter hold 80 statements; replayed as printed, 40 of the 80 matched the book's output with Python 3.14.6 and the newest packages (52 ran without an exception and 28 raised), 40 without OpenCV, 41 with PyScreeze 0.1.28, 40 under Python 3.12.3 with Tk 8.6.14 (53 ran and 27 raised) and 1 in an empty environment; the statements that differ are the pointer positions, the pixel((50, 200)) call, the Box values, the window objects, mouseInfo() and the spiralDraw.py listing, which raises IndentationError as printed [P01] [P05].
The links of the chapter

Of the 13 external links of the chapter, 7 answered 200, 3 answered 302 with a Location (the Udemy course, mouseinfo.readthedocs.io and pyautogui.readthedocs.io), youtu.be answered 303 and then 429, the sushigoroundbot repository answered 403 through the proxy of this study, and sumopaint.com was unreachable with an SSLError [P01] [P43].
The online materials

The online materials of the 3rd edition (7,759,877 bytes, 91 files, 72 of them Python) hold spiralDraw.py (580 bytes, 15 lines) as the only file that imports pyautogui and five files that import pyperclip (alternatingText.py, ccwd.py, cliprec.py, phoneAndEmail.py and showmap.py), and none of pyautogui.py, submit.png, screenshot.png or mouseInfoLog.txt, which the chapter names; the publisher's book page has 1 occurrence of Controlling the Keyboard and Mouse and 0 of PyAutoGUI [P01] [P02] [P04].
The pixel call

pixel(0, 0) returned RGB(red=176, green=176, blue=175) as the chapter prints, but pixel((50, 200)), the second form the chapter prints, raised TypeError: pixel() missing 1 required positional argument: 'y'; pixelMatchesColor was True for (130, 135, 144), False for (131, 135, 144) and True with tolerance=1, and a display of depth 16 returned (172, 174, 172) for a background of (176, 176, 175) and failed the match (MEASURED single runs) [P01] [P11] [P18].
The spiral

The chapter's spiral loop made 32 drag calls, the first five (300, 0), (0, 280), (-280, 0), (0, -260) and (260, 0), and drew inside the box (180, 129, 481, 411); the shipped spiralDraw.py (580 bytes, 15 lines) drew inside the same box and exited with 0, but it calls dragRel, waits with time.sleep(5), sets LOG_SCREENSHOTS and uses a duration of 0.1 where the chapter prints drag and 0.2 (MEASURED single runs) [P01] [P02].
Windows-only window functions

On Linux none of the 6 window functions (getActiveWindow, getAllWindows, getWindowsAt, getWindowsWithTitle, getAllTitles and getActiveWindowTitle) exists in pyautogui 0.9.54, importing pygetwindow 0.0.9 raises NotImplementedError, PyAutoGUI 0.9.40 does not import at all, and both the PyAutoGUI documentation (Windows-only, currently) and the PyGetWindow README (only the Windows platform is implemented) say so; the chapter's listings 17, 18 and 19 therefore raise at their first getActiveWindow call [P01] [P07] [P23].
XTEST and sent events

Input from PyAutoGUI reached an X window with send_event False through the XTEST extension, the letter q sent with XSendEvent arrived with send_event True, and xterm discarded the 2 keystrokes ab sent with XSendEvent, received cd from PyAutoGUI and received ab only with allowSendEvents true (MEASURED single runs) [P31] [P32] [P42] [P56].

nodes.label: Installing and sending input
nodes.body: The opening of the chapter defines graphical user interface automation, or GUI automation, as programs that do what a human user at the computer can do with the mouse and keyboard, says the PyAutoGUI library provides it, warns not to save a program as pyautogui.py, and explains that macOS lets a program control the mouse and keyboard only after the program running the script is allowed as an accessibility application (Sweigart, 2025). The PyAutoGUI documentation says the library works on Windows, macOS and Linux and lists the packages Linux needs, among them scrot and python3-tk (PyAutoGUI documentation, 2026).

The PyAutoGUI documentation says the library works on Windows, macOS and Linux and lists the packages Linux needs, among them scrot and python3-tk (PyAutoGUI documentation, 2026).

Three ideas carry this subject: the libraries that were installed and what the chapter's wording of their versions means, the way each operating system accepts synthetic input, and the permissions that decide whether the input is accepted. This study ran Python 3.14.6, installed with uv, with PyAutoGUI 0.9.54 on Ubuntu 24.04 inside a private virtual X display (Xvfb with openbox), which is a stand-in and not a real screen; the Windows and macOS paths and a real Wayland session were NOT EXECUTED (This study, 2026). nodes.label: Windows and keyboard
nodes.body: The chapter says image recognition is fragile and window features are faster and more reliable, notes that as of PyAutoGUI 1.0.0 they work only on Windows, lists the attributes of a Window object, and then teaches write(), key names, keyDown(), keyUp(), press() and hotkey() (Sweigart, 2025). The PyGetWindow README says it is still under development and that currently only the Windows platform is implemented (PyGetWindow documentation, 2026).

paras.text: The chapter says image recognition is fragile and window features are faster and more reliable, notes that as of PyAutoGUI 1.0.0 they work only on Windows, lists the attributes of a Window object, and then teaches write(), key names, keyDown(), keyUp(), press() and hotkey() (Sweigart, 2025). The PyGetWindow README says it is still under development and that currently only the Windows platform is implemented (PyGetWindow documentation, 2026).

Four ideas carry this subject: the window objects, the typing of text, the key names and the hotkeys with their focus. Everything on the keyboard was observed as key events in a Tk window, and the window objects of Windows were NOT EXECUTED (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Window objects
nodes.body: The chapter shows getActiveWindow() returning a Win32Window with left, top, width, height, size, topleft, center, box and title, and states that these features work only on Windows as of version 1.0.0 (Sweigart, 2025). The PyAutoGUI documentation lists the window feature as Windows-only, currently (PyAutoGUI documentation, 2026).

On Linux none of the six names getActiveWindow, getAllWindows, getWindowsAt, getWindowsWithTitle, getAllTitles and getActiveWindowTitle exists in pyautogui 0.9.54, calling pyautogui.getActiveWindow() raised AttributeError, and import pygetwindow with PyGetWindow 0.0.9 raised NotImplementedError: PyGetWindow currently does not support Linux (This study, 2026). The chapter's listings 17, 18 and 19 are the ones with window objects, and each raised at its first getActiveWindow call (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Typing text
nodes.body: The chapter says write() sends virtual key presses to the active window, that an optional second argument pauses between characters, that a list of key names can be passed instead of a string, and that characters such as A or ! are typed with SHIFT held (Sweigart, 2025). The PyAutoGUI documentation describes the write function and its interval argument (PyAutoGUI documentation, 2026).

Four leaves cover it: the string, the interval, the list of names and the shift key. They were run against an entry and a text box of Tk on the virtual display (This study, 2026).

nodes.label: Write string
nodes.body: The chapter types Hello, world! with pyautogui.click(100, 200); pyautogui.write('Hello, world!'), and says that by default the full string is entered instantly (Sweigart, 2025). The PyAutoGUI documentation says the primary keyboard function is write (PyAutoGUI documentation, 2026).

nodes.body: The chapter says that keys such as SHIFT are represented by short strings like 'esc' and 'enter', that pyautogui.KEYBOARD_KEYS lists all the possible strings, and that 'shift', 'ctrl', 'alt' and 'win' refer to the left-side key; it prints Table 23-1 (Sweigart, 2025). nodes.body: The chapter says a hotkey is a combination of key presses, that hotkey() presses its arguments in order and releases them in reverse order, and that the active window is the one that accepts keyboard input (Sweigart, 2025). The PyAutoGUI documentation lists hotkey as taking a list of key names (PyAutoGUI documentation, 2026).

nodes.label: Focus decides
nodes.body: The chapter says the active window accepts keyboard input, that write() depends on which window is active and has focus, and that a mouse click should be sent first to make sure the text field has focus; it keeps click and write on one line so that no other window comes into focus between them (Sweigart, 2025). The Xlib manual has an event mask, FocusChangeMask, for any change in input focus (X.Org Foundation, 2026).

lecture.title: Chapter 23: Controlling the Keyboard and Mouse
lecture.say: This chapter is about a program that controls the keyboard and the mouse, which is called GUI automation. It has fifteen examples, and all of them run on the chapter page in the order of this deck. The examples run PyAutoGUI on a private virtual display, so nothing is sent to the screen of the machine and a small window reports every event it receives. Windows and macOS were not run. The route on slide 2 shows the five parts, and the questions on slide 3 say what the chapter answers.

lecture.title: Today's route through five parts
lecture.say: The chapter has five parts. Part 1 starts the display, shows what fails without one, and shows that a window receives a real click. Part 2 covers the pause after each call and the four corners that stop a script. Part 3 moves, clicks, drags and scrolls the mouse. Part 4 takes screenshots and searches the screen for a picture. Part 5 types text, names keys, presses combinations and reads the clipboard. The summary and the links come last, and the questions on slide 3 tell you what to look for in each part.

lecture.title: Two questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: Two questions frame the chapter. The first asks how a script's click reaches a window and what stops a script that has gone wrong. Parts 1 and 2 answer it with a window that logs its events and with the four fail-safe corners, and the summary on slide 40 repeats it. The second asks which calls fail quietly, with no error and no effect. The table on slide 38 collects four of them, and the practice questions on slide 39 let you check yourself.

lecture.title: Part 1: The display, the session and the first input
lecture.say: Part 1 starts with the display, because every call of the chapter needs one. The first example prints the versions that run and asks the display for its size and the pointer for its position. The second example removes the display and shows the error, and it also shows that a Wayland session refuses a screenshot. The third example shows that a window receives a click as a real button event, and that a key sent in another way carries a flag. See the concept slide 5 for the terms.

lecture.title: Installing, the display and the session
lecture.say: Four ideas come before the first call. pyautogui sends input to the display, so a script needs a display, and on macOS the user must allow the program in the accessibility settings. The input goes to the window that is active, so the script has to make sure that the right window is there. The screen has an origin at the top left, and a display scale above 100 percent changes the numbers. Selenium and logging are named here as the alternatives for browsers and for records. Slide 7 prints the versions and the size.

lecture.title: Story: An email of 19 June 1984 introduced the window system X
lecture.say: On 19 June 1984 Robert W. Scheifler sent an email in which he said that he had spent a couple of weeks writing a window system for the VS100. He had taken a fair amount of code from a system called W, had given it an asynchronous interface and had called it X, and he wrote that it appeared to be about twice as fast as W. The picture shows a desktop of X. The display of the examples is an X display, so slide 9 shows what its windows receive.

lecture.title: Which versions run, and does the display answer?
lecture.say: The first printed line is the version of Python, 3.14.6. The second is the list of versions: pyautogui 0.9.54, pyscreeze 1.0.1, pillow 13.0.0 and pymsgbox 2.0.1. PyAutoGUI is still below 1.0.0, which matters for slide 29, because the book says a search returned None before version 1.0.0. The display answers size() with a width of 1920 and a height of 1080, and the pointer starts at 960 and 540, the middle of the display. The next slide shows what happens without a display.

lecture.title: What happens when no screen is there?
lecture.say: Without a DISPLAY variable the import of pyautogui stops at once with a KeyError for DISPLAY. A session of type Wayland answers screenshot() with a PyScreeze exception, because the screenshot tools do not work there. The same code on an X display returns the size, 1920 by 1080. This matters for a script that runs from a scheduler or from a remote shell, where no display exists. The display of the examples is a virtual one; slide 9 shows what a window receives on it, and slide 6 tells where the X system came from.

lecture.title: Does the window know the input is synthetic?
lecture.say: A click made by PyAutoGUI reaches the window as a press and a release of button 1, and the flag send_event is False: the X server itself made the event, so the window cannot tell it from a real mouse. The key w arrives the same way. A key sent with a SendEvent request arrives with the flag True, which a program can refuse. Both letters reached the entry, which printed wq. Slide 6 tells the story of the X system, and slide 14 returns to the safeguards.

lecture.title: Part 2: Pauses and fail-safes
lecture.say: Part 2 is about the two safeguards of PyAutoGUI. The first is a pause of 0.1 seconds after most calls, which gives a person time to react and which the first example measures. The second is the fail-safe: a pointer in one of the four corners of the screen makes the next call raise an exception. The second example tries three positions and also shows what a change of the screen size does to the corners of a script that is already running. Slide 11 explains the terms.

lecture.title: Pauses and fail-safes protect a running script
lecture.say: Two safeguards are named in this part. PAUSE is the number of seconds that pyautogui waits after most calls, and its default is 0.1. FailSafeException is raised when the pointer is in a corner of the screen, and it exists so that a person can stop a script by moving the mouse to a corner. sleep() and countdown() wait on purpose, and the looking-busy program moves the pointer a little so that the computer does not count the user as idle. Slide 13 measures the pause and slide 14 the corners.

lecture.title: Story: A wreck in 1918 spurred train devices that stop without an operator
lecture.say: A dead man's switch is a device that stops a machine when the person who operates it can no longer do so. The Malbone Street Wreck of 1918 on the Brooklyn Rapid Transit system was not caused by the illness of a driver, but it spurred the wide use of such devices on trains. The picture shows the pedal of a German train safety system. The corners of the screen do the same for a script, and slide 14 shows them at work.

lecture.title: PAUSE: a wait after most calls
lecture.say: The first line shows the defaults: PAUSE is 0.1 and FAILSAFE is True. The pause was raised to 0.3 seconds to make it easy to measure. moveTo(), click() and press() waited after the call, which printed True. position() and onScreen() did not wait, which printed False, because they only ask and do nothing to the screen. So a slow script is slowed by its actions and not by its questions. Slide 14 shows the second safeguard, the corners, and slide 11 explains both.

lecture.title: The four corners stop a runaway script
lecture.say: The four fail-safe points are the corners of the screen: (0, 0), (0, 1079), (1919, 0) and (1919, 1079). A pointer at (0, 0) or at (1919, 1079) made the next call raise FailSafeException, and a pointer at (1, 1), one pixel inside, did not. After the display was resized to 1280 by 720, the running process still held the corners of 1920 by 1080, and a new process held 1279 and 719. A script should read the size again after a change. See slide 12 for the story of the safety idea.

lecture.title: Part 3: Moving, clicking, dragging, scrolling
lecture.say: Part 3 controls the mouse. The first example counts the small steps that a move takes for five durations and shows what happens with a target outside the screen. The second example sends six kinds of click and prints the button events that arrived. The third example draws the book's spiral with drag() and reads the drawing back from the display. The fourth example scrolls under two versions of the Tk toolkit and counts the lines that moved. Slide 16 lists the calls.

lecture.title: The mouse: ideas and calls
lecture.say: The mouse calls fall into two groups. Moving: moveTo() goes to a point, move() goes by a distance, and position() reports where the pointer is, with duration spreading the move over time. Interacting: click() sends a press and a release, with button, clicks and interval changing what is sent, and drag() and dragTo() move with the button held down, while scroll() turns the wheel. MouseInfo, which needs the Tk toolkit, shows coordinates and colors for planning. Slides 19 to 22 print the effect of each call.

lecture.title: The mouse: calls, figures and options
lecture.say: The second part of the mouse table lists the calls themselves. position() returns the pointer as a tuple with x and y, click() takes button, clicks and interval, and drag() and dragTo() hold the button down while they move. mouseInfo() opens the MouseInfo window when the Tk toolkit is present. The two figures show the book's spiral and the MouseInfo window, and spiralDraw.py is the program behind the spiral. The arguments duration and button change how long a move takes and which button is sent. See the previous slide for the ideas.

lecture.title: Story: The mouse was shown in public on 9 December 1968
lecture.say: On 14 November 1963 Douglas Engelbart wrote in his notebook about a pointing device that he called a bug, and Bill English helped him to build the first prototype in 1964. Engelbart showed the mouse in public on 9 December 1968. The picture shows a prototype. The calls of this part move a pointer, press its buttons and turn its wheel, which are the things that device first made possible. Slide 19 starts with the first call.

lecture.title: moveTo(): how many steps does a move take?
lecture.say: The chart counts the small steps, which are motion events that the window received, for five durations. Duration 0 and 0.1 gave one event, 0.25 gave 6, 0.5 gave 11 and 1.0 gave 21, so a longer move makes more steps. A move that is shorter than the minimum step jumps in one event. A target outside the screen was cut to the nearest point: (-50, -50) ended at (0, 0) and (5000, 5000) ended at (1919, 1079). The fail-safe was switched off for that test. Slide 20 continues with clicks.

lecture.title: click(): which button events does each call send?
lecture.say: Each call sent its own events. click() sent one press of button 1. click(button='middle') sent button 2 and rightClick() sent button 3. doubleClick() sent a press and a double click event, and tripleClick() added a triple click event. click(clicks=2, interval=0.6) sent two single presses, because the second click came too late to count as a double click. A program that reacts to double clicks therefore needs the default interval. Slide 21 continues with the drag.

lecture.title: drag(): the book's spiral, drawn on the display
lecture.say: The example draws the book's square spiral. Each drag() is relative to the pointer, so the program goes right, down, left and up, and each side is 20 pixels shorter than the one before. Thirty-two calls were made, and thirty of them pressed and released the button; the last two had no distance left. The ink fills a box from (200, 159) to (501, 441), which is the picture that the window drew. Every press had its release, so the button was never left down. Slide 22 turns to scrolling.

lecture.title: scroll(): how many lines is one click?
lecture.say: The chart and the table show how many lines one scroll moved. Under Tk 9.0.3, scroll(-1) moved 1 line, -2 moved 3, -3 moved 5 and -10 moved 19. Under Tk 8.6.14 the same calls moved 2, 5, 8 and 29 lines. So the unit of a click depends on the toolkit of the window, and the same script scrolls a different distance in another program. Test the distance where the script will run, and compare slide 19 for the pointer moves.

lecture.title: Part 4: The screen: pictures and finding a button
lecture.say: Part 4 is about the screen. A screenshot is a Pillow picture of the whole display, so everything that you can do with a picture applies. The first example reads one pixel and tests a color with a tolerance. The second example cuts a button out of a screenshot and searches for it, which also shows how a found box becomes a click position. The third example changes one pixel and searches again in three environments, to show when nothing is found. Slide 24 explains the terms.

lecture.title: The screen: pictures, pixels and image search
lecture.say: The screen calls fall into three groups. screenshot() returns a picture, pixel() returns the color of one point, and pixelMatchesColor() tests a color with a tolerance. locateOnScreen() searches the screen for a small picture and returns its box, locateAllOnScreen() returns every box, and newer versions raise ImageNotFoundException when nothing is found. Window objects, with getActiveWindow() and getWindowsWithTitle(), work on Windows only, so they were not run here. Slides 27 to 29 print the results of the screen calls.

lecture.title: The screen: windows and the book's pictures
lecture.say: The second part of the screen table is about windows and the book's picture files. Window objects hold the title, the position and the size of a window, and getActiveWindow() and getWindowsWithTitle() find them. These calls work on Windows only, so they were not run here. The book names its saved screenshot screenshot.png and its button picture submit.png. The figure of the Mu editor shows a window before and after its attributes change. Compare the previous slide for the calls that work on every system.

lecture.title: Story: The word CAPTCHA was coined in 2003 for a test that bots fail
lecture.say: In 2003 Luis von Ahn, Manuel Blum, Nicholas Hopper and John Langford coined the word CAPTCHA, which stands for a completely automated public test to tell computers and humans apart. Such a test exists to deter bot attacks and spam. The picture shows one. A script that takes a screenshot receives only a picture of the screen, and nothing in PyAutoGUI reads the picture for it, which slide 27 shows by printing the type of the result.

lecture.title: screenshot() and pixel(): what the screen shows
lecture.say: The screenshot is a PNG image object of 1920 by 1080 pixels in mode RGB. pixel(210, 160) returned the color (176, 176, 175), the grey of the window background, and the pixel at (5, 5) was black, the background of the display. pixelMatchesColor() returned True for an exact color, False for a color one step off with tolerance 0, and True with tolerance 1. pixel((210, 160)) with a tuple raised TypeError, because the call wants two numbers. Slide 28 searches the screen for a picture.

lecture.title: locateOnScreen(): where is the button?
lecture.say: The button was cut out of a screenshot and saved as submit.png. locateOnScreen() found it at left 300 and top 250, 84 pixels wide and 35 high, and locateAllOnScreen() found two identical buttons, the second at top 330. The center of the first box is (342, 267). click() accepts a box, so click(boxes[1]) pressed the second button, which the window reported. The red box in the picture marks the first match. Slide 29 changes one pixel and shows what then happens.

lecture.title: When does locateOnScreen() find nothing?
lecture.say: Three environments searched for the same button in four ways. With OpenCV, the exact picture was found and a picture with one changed pixel raised ImageNotFound, while confidence=0.9 found it again. Without OpenCV, confidence raised NotImplemented, because the match needs OpenCV. With PyScreeze 0.1.28, a failed search returned None and did not raise anything, which is the behavior that the book describes for versions before 1.0.0. Slide 7 shows the versions that were used.

lecture.title: Part 5: The keyboard and the clipboard
lecture.say: Part 5 controls the keyboard. The first example types a text into a window, types a list that holds key names, holds a key down and presses a combination. The second example gives a key name that does not exist and a letter that the layout does not know, and shows that nothing is raised. The third example presses a combination, copies the text of the window and reads it back through the clipboard. Slide 31 explains the calls and slide 38 collects the quiet failures.

lecture.title: The keyboard: typing, keys and hotkeys
lecture.say: The keyboard calls fall into three groups. write() types the characters of a str or of a list, press() sends one key by name from KEYBOARD_KEYS, and keyDown() and keyUp() hold and release a key. hotkey() presses a combination such as ctrl and c, and pyperclip reads the clipboard that the combination filled. alert(), confirm(), prompt() and password() show boxes through PyMsgBox. The book's bot and clipboard programs use these calls. Slides 34 to 37 print what the window received, and slide 38 lists what fails quietly.

lecture.title: Message boxes, the clipboard and practice programs
lecture.say: The second part of the keyboard table lists the message boxes, the helper modules and the two practice programs. alert(), confirm(), prompt() and password() show a box and return what the person chose or typed, through the PyMsgBox package. pyperclip copies to the clipboard and reads from it, and KEYBOARD_KEYS lists the names that press() accepts. The figure shows an editor window that receives a click and then typed text. The practice programs read a text field through the clipboard and play a game with image search. See the previous slide for typing and hotkeys.

lecture.title: Story: The QWERTY layout was sold on a typewriter from 1874
lecture.say: Christopher Latham Sholes devised the QWERTY layout in the early 1870s. E. Remington and Sons bought the manufacturing rights of the Sholes and Glidden typewriter in 1873 and sold it from 1874, and the layout became popular with the Remington No. 2 of 1878. The picture shows the machine of 1873. A script does not press positions on a layout: write() sends characters and press() sends names, which slide 34 shows.

lecture.title: write(): typing into a window
lecture.say: write() typed 'Hello, world!' into the window, and the window's text agrees. A list may hold key names: after a, b, left, left, X and Y the text is 'Hello, world!XYab', so the two left keys moved the cursor to the start of the line. Holding shift while pressing 4 typed a dollar sign. hotkey('ctrl', 'a') followed by delete emptied the window. The picture shows the window after the text was typed again. Slide 35 shows what happens with a key name that does not exist.

lecture.title: What happens with a wrong key name?
lecture.say: KEYBOARD_KEYS holds 194 names. press('nokey') and keyDown('nokey') raised nothing and typed nothing, so a wrong name fails silently. The list write(['a', 'nokey', 'b']) typed a and b only, and write('café') typed 'caf', so the letter é never arrived. The capital 'A' is not in the list, because capitals are made with shift. A script should read the text back and compare it with what it meant to type. Slide 38 collects this with other quiet failures.

lecture.title: Story: Control-Alt-Delete was devised in 1981 to restart a computer without switching it off
lecture.say: David Bradley, the chief engineer of the IBM PC project, devised in 1981 a keyboard command that restarted the computer without switching it off. His first choice was too easy to bump, so Mel Hallerman suggested Control, Alt and Delete, which the first keyboard made hard to press with one hand. It began as a tool for the people who wrote programs, and IBM's technical reference made it known to everyone. The picture shows that keyboard. The example on slide 37 presses a combination with hotkey() in the same way: the keys go down in order and come up in reverse.

lecture.title: hotkey() and the clipboard
lecture.say: hotkey('ctrl', 'alt', 'shift', 's') pressed the four keys down in the order Control, Alt, Shift, S and released them in the reverse order, S, Shift, Alt, Control. Then ctrl and a selected all, ctrl and c copied, and pyperclip.paste() returned the two lines 'Hello, world!' and 'second line'. Pressing end and then ctrl and v pasted the text again, so the window now held the text twice, which printed True. The clipboard here is the X selection read by xclip. See slide 37 for the key order.

lecture.title: Four quiet surprises, measured by the run
lecture.say: The table collects four results that the run measured. press('nokey') raised nothing and typed an empty text, and write('café') raised nothing and typed 'caf'. A search for the exact picture returned a box, and a search for the picture with one changed pixel raised ImageNotFound. The two quiet calls give no sign, so the script has to check the result itself: read the text back, or test the box. The loud calls are easier, because the exception can be caught. See slides 35 and 29 for the examples.

lecture.title: Practice Questions
lecture.say: These are the practice questions, and each points to the part where the idea was shown. The first is about the display and the Wayland session, slides 7 and 8. The second is about the four corners and the resize, slide 14. The third is about the number of motion events and the click calls, slides 19 and 20. The fourth is about the exact match and OpenCV, slide 29. The fifth is about the wrong key name and the order of the hotkey, slides 35 and 37. Run the examples on the chapter page to check each answer.

lecture.title: Summary
lecture.say: Four claims carry the chapter. A display decides whether the script can start, and the window receives real events. PAUSE and the four corners are the safeguards. A screenshot is a picture, and a search for a picture needs an exact match unless OpenCV and a confidence are used. A wrong key name and some characters are skipped without any error, so the script must read back what arrived. These are the answers to the two questions on slide 3, and the links on slide 41 lead further.
